stem_md:
Given is a prime number  $p$  and natural  $n$  such that  $p \geq n \geq 3$ . Set  $A$  is made of sequences of lenght  $n$  with elements from the set  $\{0,1,2,...,p-1\}$  and have the following property:
  For arbitrary two sequence  $(x_1,...,x_n)$  and  $(y_1,...,y_n)$  from the set  $A$  there exist three different numbers  $k,l,m$  such that:
 $x_k \not = y_k$ ,  $x_l \not = y_l$ ,  $x_m \not = y_m$ .
Find the largest possible cardinality of  $A$ .
solution_md:
Someone has asked me to translate the official solution.

Answer:  $p^{n-2}$ 

All pairs of sequences in set  $A$  have to differ on at least one of the beggining  $n-2$  positions. Therefore the number of sequences in this set is not greater than the number of all sequences of the length  $(n-2)$  with the elements in the set of cardinality  $p$ , equivalently the number  $p^{n-2}$ .
We will construct  $p^{n-2}$  sequences with the elements in the set  $S={0, 1, 2, ..., p-1}$  which have the required property. Consider all sequences  $(x_{1}, x_{2}, ..., x_{n})$  with the elements in the set  $S$  which satisfy following conditions: $(1) x_{n-1}\equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n-2}x_{i}\mod{p}$ 
and $(2) x_{n}\equiv \sum_{i=1}^{n-2}ix_{1}\mod{p}$ 
There are  $p^{n-2}$  such sequences because every sequence  $(x_{1}, x_{2}, ...., x_{n-2})$  with the elements from the set  $S$  with the cardinality  $p$  determines the value of  $x_{n-1}$  and  ${x_{n}}$ .
Every two sequences satisfying  $(1)$  differ on at least one of the first  $n-2$  positions. We want to prove that all pairs of sequences  $(x_{1}, x_{2}, ..., x_{n})$  and  $(y_{1}, y_{2}, ..., y_{n})$  differ on at least three positions.
If these sequences differ on at least three positions of the first  $n-2$  positions there is nothing to prove. So we have to consider two cases:
1. The segments  $(x_{1}, x_{2}, ..., x_{n-2})$  and  $(y_{1}, y_{2}, ..., y_{n-2})$  differ on the exactly two positions with numbers  $i, j$  ( $1 \leq i < j \leq n-2$ ).
Then  $x_{i}\not = y_{i}$  and  $x_{j}\not = y_{j}$ . From  $(1)$  we have:
 $x_{n-1}-y_{n-1}\equiv (x_{i}-y_{i})+(x_{j}-y_{j}) \mod{p}$  $x_{n}-y_{n}\equiv i(x_{i}-y_{i})+j(x_{j}-y_{j}) \mod{p}$ 

From this we have  $(x_{n}-y_{n})-i(x_{n-1}-y_{n-1})\equiv (j-i)(x_{j}-y_{j}) \mod{p}$ . $p$  is a prime number, the numbers  $x_{j}$  and  $y_{j}$  are different and they belong to the set  $S$ . This implies that  $(x_{n}-y_{n})-i(x_{n-1}-y_{n-1})$  is not divisible by  $p$ . So one of the numbers  $x_{n-1}-y_{n-1}$  or  $x_{n}-y_{n}$  is not divisible by  $p$ . Therefore  $x_{n-1}\not = y_{n_{1}}$  or  $x_{n}\not = y_{n}$ . So our sequences differ on the position with number  $n-1$  or on the position with number  $n$ , so together they differ on at least three positions.

2. Segments  $(x_{1}, x_{2}, ..., x_{n-2})$  and  $(y_{1}, y_{2}, ..., y_{n-2}$  differ on exactly one position with the number  $i$  ( $1 \leq i \leq n-2$ ).
Then  $x_{i}\not = y_{1}$  and similary using  $(1)$  we have: $x_{n-1}-y_{n-1}\equiv x_{i}-y_{1}\mod{p}$  $x_{n}-y_{n}\equiv i(x_{i}-y_{i}) \mod{p}$ 
This implies that  numbers  $x_{n-1}-y_{n-1}$  and  $x_{n}-y_{n}$  are not divisible by  $p$ . So  $x_{n-1}\not = y_{n-1}$  and  $x_{n}\not = y_{n}$  and also in this case our sequences differ on at least three positions.

if we define the distance between two of the sequences to be the number of positions where the two sequences differ, then the problem asks for the maximum number of codewords(or sequences) of length  $n$  with a minimum distance of  $\ge 3$ .
if we delete some two co-ordinates from the  $n$  coordinates we note that the sequences are still distinct(else some two of them had a distance of atmost two) and so the maximum number of sequences is atmost  $p^{n-2}$ .
for an attainment of this bound, consider all the distinct two dimensional vector spaces over  $\mathbb{F}_p$ . there are  $\frac{p^2-1}{p-1}=p+1$  such subspaces. Let  $H$  be the matrix with  $n$  of these as columns(since  $n \le p$  this is always ok). let  $\mathcal{C}$  be the set of all vectors satisfying  $H\bold{x} =\bold{0}$ . If among the vectors of  $\mathcal{C}$  there is one with  $\leq 2$  non-zero terms, then the corresponding columns of  $H$  are linearly dependent and that is a contradiction by the construction of  $H$ . stem_md:
An equilateral triangle with side  $n$  is built with  $n^{2}$  *plates* - equilateral triangles with side  $1$ . Each plate has one side black, and the other side white. We name *the move* the following operation: we choose a plate  $P$ , which has common sides with at least two plates, whose visible side is the same color as the visible side of  $P$ . Then, we turn over plate  $P$ .

For any  $n\geq 2$  decide whether there exists an innitial configuration of plates permitting for an infinite sequence of moves.
solution_md: We name the plate which the problem says it's turnable $ good $ . We define $ degree $ of the plate $ P $ : the number of its neighbors whose visible color is as the same as the visible color $ P $ ( $ D_P $ ) . And let $ S $ be the sum of all plates' degrees. It's obvious that $ S\geq0. $ Let $ P $ be a good plate that is not on the sides of the main triangle. There's 2 possible conditions: $ i) D_P=2 $ or $ ii)D_P=3 $ In the first condition, when we turn $ P $ , its degree wanes $1$ unit and the degree of each of its homochromatic neighbors wanes $1$ unit and the degree of its non-homochromatic neighbor increases $1$ unit. So, $ S $ wanes $2$ units. In the second condition, when we turn $ P $ , its degree wanes $3$ units and the degree of each of its neighbors wanes $1$ unit. So, $ S $ wanes $6$ units. Now, consider the plates on the sides of the main triangle. The head triangles won't move; because they have only $1$ neighbor. Assume $ Q $ a good plate on a side of the main triangle. So, it's $2$ neighbors are homochromatic with $ Q $ . When we turn $ Q $ , its degree wanes $2$ units and the degree of each of its neighbors wanes $1$ unit. So, $ S $ wanes $4$ units.**So**, after each movement, $ S $ wanes. So, in order to $ S\geq0 $ and $ S $ is finite, we get that the number of possible movements is finite. So, there doesn't exist any initial configuration of plates permitting for an infinite sequence of moves.

stem_md:
$a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$ ,  $d$  are positive integers and
\[ad=b^{2}+bc+c^{2}\]
Prove that
\[a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}\]
is a composed number.
solution_md:
Hmm so while waiting in line during Black-Friday-at-eight-o-clock shopping I somehow managed to solve this one after also previously having gotten [this one](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?f=36&t=276020).  Guess that says something about how long the line was.

Note that  $2ad=2b^2+2bc+2c^2\implies 2ad-b^2-c^2=(b+c)^2$ .  Therefore \begin{align*}a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2&= a^2+2ad+d^2+b^2+c^2-2ad&=(a+d)^2-(b+c)^2&= (a+b+c+d)(a+d-b-c).\end{align*}  Since  $a,b,c,d>0$  and  $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2>0$ , in order to show that this is composite we must show that  $a+d=b+c+1$  is not possible.  Suppose it is possible.  Then squaring yields \[a^2+2ad+d^2=b^2+2bc+c^2+2b+2c+1\implies a^2+ad+d^2=bc+2b+2c+1.\]  Using the fact that  $ad=b^2+bc+c^2$  again gives \[a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2+ad+bc=ad+bc+2b+2c+1\implies a^2+(b-1)^2+(c-1)^2+d^2=1.\]  However, since  $a^2+d^2\geq 2$  we have a contradiction.  Therefore  $a+d-b-c\geq 2$  and  $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$  is composite, as desired.   $\blacksquare$
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Poland Contests/Poland - Second Round/2007 Poland - Second Round/136141.json

Set  $p = a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}.$  Next assume  $p$  is a prime. Then 

\begin{eqnarray*}p & = & (a^{2}+2ad+d^{2})+(b^{2}+c^{2}-2ad)  & = & (a+d)^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}-2(b^{2}+c^{2}+bc)  & = & (a+d)^{2}-(b^{2}+2bc+c^{2})  & = & (a+d)^{2}-(b+c)^{2} & = & (a-b-c+d)(a+b+c+d). \end{eqnarray*}

Since  $p$  is a prime, the only possible factorization af  $p$  is  $1 \cdot p$ . Hence  $a-b-c+d = 1$  and  $a+b+c+d = p$ , which implies that  $a+d ={\textstyle \frac{p+1}{2}}$  and  $b+c ={\textstyle \frac{p-1}{2}}$ . Now 
 ${\textstyle \frac{(p+1)^{2}}{16}\; = \; (\frac{a+d}{2})^{2}\geq ad \;=\; b^{2}+c^{2}+bc \; \geq \; \frac{3}{4}(b+c)^{2}\; = \; \frac{3(p-1)^{2}}{16}.}$ 

This gives the following chain of implications: 

\begin{eqnarray*}{\textstyle \frac{(p+1)^{2}}{16}}& \geq &{\textstyle \frac{3(p-1)^{2}}{16}} 3(p-1)^{2}-(p+1)^{2}& \leq & 0  p^{2}-4p+1 & \leq & 0  p & < & 4 \end{eqnarray*}

Therefore 
 ${\textstyle b+c \;=\; \frac{p-1}{2}\; \leq \; \frac{3-1}{2}\;=\; 1.}$ 

But  $b$  and  $c$  are positive integers, so  $b+c \geq 2.$  This contradiction implies that  $p$  is a composite number.

[http://www.mathlinks.ro/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=136491](http://www.mathlinks.ro/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=136491)

Note that 
\[(a+d)^2 - (b+c)^2 = a^2+d^2 + 2(ad-bc) - b^2-c^2 = a^2+d^2 + 2(b^2+c^2)-b^2-c^2 = a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2\]
Thus,  $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2 = (a+d-b-c)\cdot (a+d+b+c)$ . Thus, it suffices to show that  $a+d\geq b+c+2$ . AFTSOC that  $a+d\leq b+c+1$ , then 
\[b^2+bc+c^2=ad\leq \frac{(a+d)^2}{4} \leq \frac{(b+c+1)^2}{4}\]
So, 
\[4b^2+4bc+4c^2\leq b^2+c^2+2bc+2b+2c+1\]
Then,
\[3b^2+2bc+3c^2\leq 2b+2c+1\]
but since  $b,c$  are positive, we have  $3b^2>2b, 2bc>1, 3c^2>2c$ , so this is absurd. Thus,  $(a+d-b-c)\geq 2$ , so  $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$  can be written as the product of two integers  $\geq 2$  and we're done.

solution_md: Let $X = AD \cap CE, Y = AC \cap BD, Z = AS \cap CD$ . Observe trivially that $AEDS$ and $ABCS$ are cyclic. We then make the following observations:**Claim:** $SYCZ$ and $SXDZ$ are cyclic. *Proof:* We have that \[\angle BCA = \angle BSA = \angle DSZ = \angle YCZ.\] A similar angle chase ensues for $SXDZ$ . $\square$ **Claim:** $AXSY$ and $DXYC$ are cyclic. *Proof:* We have that \begin{align*} \angle CSY &= 180^{\circ} - (\angle BSA + \angle ASE) &= 180^{\circ} - (\angle YCD + \angle XDZ) &= \angle DAC \implies AXSY \text{ is cyclic.} \end{align*} Hence we then have that \[\angle AYX = \angle ASX = \angle ZDX \implies DXYC \text{ is cyclic. } \square \] Now observe that \begin{align*} \angle SYC &= \angle SYZ + \angle ZYC &= \angle XCD + \angle ZSC &= \angle XYD + \angle XSA &= \angle XYD + \angle XYA &= \angle SYA, \end{align*} so that as \[\angle SYC + \angle SYA = 180^{\circ} \implies \angle SYC = 90^{\circ} \implies \angle SZC = 180^{\circ} - \angle SYC = 90^{\circ},\] as desired. $\blacksquare$

Find all functions  $ f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$  for which the equality
\[f(f(x)\minus{}y)\equal{}f(x)\plus{}f(f(y)\minus{}f(\minus{}x))\plus{}x\]
holds for all real  $x,y$ .
solution_md:
My gut says this solution is flawed, and my gut is usually right. :( But here we go anyways.
 $ x \equal{} y \equal{} 0$  gives  $ f(f(0)) \equal{} f(0) \plus{} f(0) \equal{} 2f(0)$ .  $ x \equal{} 0, y \equal{} f(0)$  gives  $ f(0) \equal{} f(0) \plus{} f(f(f(0)) \minus{} f(0))$ , or  $ 0 \equal{} f(f(f(0)) \minus{} f(0)) \equal{} f(2f(0) \minus{} f(0)) \equal{} f(f(0)) \equal{} 2f(0)$ . Thus  $ f(0) \equal{} 0$ .

Put in  $ x \equal{} 0$  and conclude that  $ f( \minus{} y) \equal{} f(f(y))$ . Take  $ f$  of both sides to get  $ f(f( \minus{} y)) \equal{} f(f(f(y)))$ , or  $ f( \minus{} ( \minus{} y)) \equal{} f(y) \equal{} f(f(f(y)))$ .

Put in  $ y \equal{} 0$  and conclude that  $ f(f(x)) \equal{} f(x) \plus{} f( \minus{} f( \minus{} x))$ . Or,  $ f(f(x)) \equal{} f(x) \plus{} f(f(f(f(x))))$ . Or,  $ f(f(x)) \equal{} f(x) \plus{} f(f(x))$ . Thus  $ f(x) \equal{} 0$  for all  $ x$ .

stem_md: We have an  $n \times n$  board, and in every square there is an integer. The sum of all integers on the board is  $0$ . We define an action on a square where the integer in the square is decreased by the number of neighbouring squares, and the number inside each of the neighbouring squares is increased by 1. Determine if there exists  $n\geq 2$  such that we can turn all the integers into zeros in a finite number of actions.
solution_md:
The problem is not that hard. I solved it on the contest, so it should be easy :wink: Well, for now I know 3 complete proofs, and one of them is I think very clever (not mine unfortunately). I'll post 2 hints for the standard solution:

<details><summary>Small Hint</summary>Try to find a good invariable :wink:</details>

<details><summary>Huge Hint</summary>Look at the longest diagonal</details>

<details><summary>Full Solution</summary>We'll prove that it is not possible for every combination of integers. Let's produce a counterexample. First see that by an action we cannot change the parity of the sum of the numbers on the longest diagonal. To prove this we only need some cases to be done (what's happening when we operate on a square on the diagonal, a square not on the long diagonal etc.). So we can produce a counterexample. Take any odd integer  $ k$ . Let us have a board with  $ k$  on the long diagonal,  $ \minus{}k$  which is not on the long diagonal and all the other integers we set as zeros. Then it's obvious that after a finite number of actions the sum of the integers on the long diagonal is still going to be odd, thus a board with only zeros will never occur due to a contradiction to the parity of the sum of the integers on the long diagonal :wink:</details>

<details><summary>Hint for solution 2</summary>Try to find a more complicated invariable mod2 working separetely for  $ n\equal{}2k$  and  $ n\equal{}2k\plus{}1$</details>

<details><summary>Hint for solution by Piotr Szcześniak</summary>Work separetely for  $ n\equal{}2k$  and  $ n\equal{}2k\plus{}1$ . Try to produce a contradiction putting only 1's and -1's into the board (for one case put only one 2 instead of 1)</details> :wink:

stem_md:
We are given a triangle  $ ABC$  such that  $ AC \equal{} BC$ . There is a point  $ D$  lying on the segment  $ AB$ , and  $ AD < DB$ . The point  $ E$  is symmetrical to  $ A$  with respect to  $ CD$ . Prove that:
\[\frac {AC}{CD} \equal{} \frac {BE}{BD \minus{} AD}\]
solution_md:
Let $ ABC$ be a $ C$ - isosceles triangle. For a point $ D\in (AB)$ , $ AD < DB$ denote the reflection $ E$ of the point $ A$ w.r.t. the line $ CD$ . Prove that $ \frac {AC}{CD} = \frac {BE}{BD - AD}$ .
**Proof.** Prove easily that $ \{\begin{array}{c} \widehat {CED}\equiv\widehat {CAD}\equiv\widehat {CBD} BC = CE = AC\ ,\ DE = AD\end{array}$ $ \implies$ $ \widehat {CED}\equiv\widehat {CBD}$ , i.e. the quadrilateral $ BCDE$ is cyclically. Apply the **Ptolemaios' theorem** in the quadrilateral $ BCDE$ : $ BC\cdot DE + CD\cdot BE = BD\cdot CE$ $ \Longleftrightarrow$ $ AC\cdot AD + CD\cdot BE = BD\cdot AC$ $ \Longleftrightarrow$ $ \boxed {\frac {AC}{CD} = \frac {BE}{BD - AD}}$ .**Remark.** If $ F\in CD\cap BE$ , then the quadrilateral $ ACBF$ is cyclically and $ \boxed {\frac {AC}{CF} = \frac {AB}{AF + BF}}$ . See [**here**](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/blog/50478).

stem_md: We have a positive integer  $ n$  such that  $ n \neq 3k$ . Prove that there exists a positive integer  $ m$  such that  $ \forall_{k\in N \ k\geq m} \ k$  can be represented as a sum of digits of some multiplication of  $ n$ .
solution_md:
Lemma: If  $ a$  and  $ b$  are positive integers that are relatively prime, for all integers  $ n$  that are bigger than  $ ab \minus{} a \minus{} b$ ,  $ ax \plus{} by \equal{} n$  has a solution such that  $ x$  and  $ y$  are nonnegative integers.
That is a well-known fact. It called Chicken Mc-nugget theorem which has been used in an old IMO problem. http://www.mathlinks.ro/viewtopic.php?p=366618#366618 First we will prove that n has two multiples such that sum of the digits of their decimal represantation are relatively prime.  $ n \equal{} 2^s5^pq$  and  $ q$  is relatively prime with  $ 10$ . From the Chinese Remainder Theorem we have posive integer  $ m$  such that  $ mq \equal{} 19(mod 100)$  and  $ m \equal{} 1(mod 3)$ . Let  $ mq$  has  $ d$  digits decimal represantation and sum of this digits is  $ t$ . Now look at the number  $ mq(10^{d \minus{} 1} \plus{} 1)$  sum of digits in its decimal represantation is  $ 2t \minus{} 9$ .  $ t$  and  $ 2t \minus{} 9$  are relatively prime because  $ t$  isn't divisible by  $ 3$ . Multiplying  $ mq$  and  $ mq(10^{d \minus{} 1} \plus{} 1)$  with a sufficiently large power of  $ 10$  we get two multiples of  $ n$  such that sum of the digits of their decimal represantation are relatively prime. 
Now  $ a$  and  $ b$  are two multiples of  $ n$  such that sum of digits in their decimal represantations(say them  $ s(a)$  and  $ s(b)$  respectively) are relatively prime. From the lemma for an integer  $ k$  which is bigger than  $ s(a)s(b) \minus{} s(a) \minus{} s(b)$  there are nonnegative integers  $ x$  and  $ y$  such that  $ s(a)x \plus{} s(b)y \equal{} k$ . Adjoin  $ x$  pieces of  $ a$  and  $ y$  pieces of  $ b$  in decimal system( $ aaa...abbb...b$ ). It has sum of digits  $ k$  and it is a multiple of  $ n$ .

stem_md: Let  $W(x)$  be a polynomial of integer coefficients such that for any pair of different rational number  $r_1$ ,  $r_2$  dependence  $W(r_1) \neq W(r_2)$  is true. Decide, whether the assuptions imply that for any pair of different real numbers  $t_1$ ,  $t_2$  dependence  $W(t_1) \neq W(t_2)$  is true.
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>False. Take  $W(x)=x^3-2x$ . Clearly the second statement is not true, so it suffices to prove that the first is.

Assume for the sake of contradiction that  ${r}^3-2{r}={s}^3-2{s}$ . Rearranging, we get  $r^3-s^3=2(r-s)$ . Dividing by  $(r-s)$ , we get  $r^2+rs+s^2=2$ . 

Since  $r$  and  $s$  are rational, we write  $r=\frac{a}{b}$  and  $s=\frac{c}{d}$  in lowest terms. So our equation becomes  $\frac{a^2}{b^2}+\frac{ac}{bd}+\frac{b^2}{d^2}=2$ , or   $$ a^2d^2+b^2c^2+abcd=2b^2d^2 $$  Note that the equation implies that at least one of  $a$  or  $d$  is even and that at least one of  $b$  or  $c$  is even. If  $a$  was even, then  $c$  would have to be even as well ( $a$  and  $b$  are relatively prime). So  $b$  and  $d$  are odd. But that would mean that the LHS is divisible by  $4$  but the RHS is not, contradiction.

So we know  $d$  was even, which implies that  $b$  is even. So we let  $d=2d'$  and  $b=2b'$  So our equation is now   $$ 4(a^2{d'^2}+{b'^2}c^2+ab'cd')=32{b'^2}{d'^2} $$  We divide by  $4$  to get   $$ a^2{d'^2}+{b'^2}c^2+ab'cd'=8{b'^2}{d'^2} $$  Since we know that  $a$  and  $c$  are odd, that implies that  $b'$  and  $d'$  are even. From here, we can use infinite descent to conclude that  $b$  and  $d$  have infinite powers of  $2$  in their prime factorization, which is a contradiction  $\blacksquare$</details>

stem_md: Decide, whether exist tetrahedrons  $T$ ,  $T'$  with walls  $S_1$ ,  $S_2$ ,  $S_3$ ,  $S_4$  and  $S_1'$ ,  $S_2'$ ,  $S_3'$ ,  $S_4'$ , respectively, such that for  $i = 1, 2, 3, 4$  triangle  $S_i$  is similar to triangle  $S_i'$ , but despite this, tetrahedron  $T$  is not similar to tetrahedron  $T'$ .
solution_md:
Call  $T= A_1A_2A_3A_4$ .
First, magnify tetrahedron  $T'$  into  $W$  such that the faces of  $W$  are congruent. Then, the volumes of the tetrahedrons are equal. But the areas of the corresponding faces are also equal. Hence, the heights of the tetrahedron are equal also. 

Take a isometry which sends  $W$  into  $B_1A_2A_3A_4$ , with  $A_1$  and  $B_1$  in the same half-plane formed by  $(A_2A_3A_4)$ . Then,  $A_1B_1 \parallel (A_2A_3A_4)$ , while  $d(A_2, (A_1A_3A_4) ) = d(A_2, (B_1A_3A_4) )$ , and analougousily for  $A_3$  and  $A_4$ . These relations imply 3 pairs of congruent triangles because the heights of the tetrahedron from  $A_1$  and  $B_1$  are congruent, and hence the projections of these points are equally distanced from the projections of  $A_2$ ,  $A_3$  and  $A_4$  on the corresponding planes. Hence, the projections coincide and so  $A_1$  and  $B_1$ . Hence, the tetrahedrons are congruent, so the answer to the problem is "there are no two tetrahedrons with the given properties".

solution_md:
Determine, whether exists function $f$ , which assigns each integer $k$ , nonnegative integer $f(k)$ and meets the conditions: $f(0) > 0$ , for each integer $k$ minimal number of the form $f(k - l) + f(l)$ , where $l \in \mathbb{Z}$ , equals $f(k)$ .
Note that $\min_{y\in Z}(f(x-y)+f(y))=f(x)$ is equivalent to : c1) $f(x+y)\le f(x)+f(y)$ $\forall x,y\in\mathbb Z$ c2) $\forall x$ , $\exists y$ such that $f(x)=f(x-y)+f(y)$ Let $m=\min_{x\in Z}f(x)$ ( $m\ge 0$ ) Let $u$ such that $f(u)=m$ Using c2, $\exists v$ such that $m=f(u)=f(u-v)+f(v)\ge 2m$ and so $m=0$ Let $A=\{x\in\mathbb Z$ such that $f(x)=0\}$ . Note that $0\notin A$ c1) implies then : c3) $a,b\in A$ implies $a+b\in A$ If all elements of $A$ are $>0$ : c2 is wrong for $x=\min (A)$ If all elements of $A$ are $<0$ : c2 is wrong for $x=\max (A)$ So $\exists a=\min(A\cap\mathbb Z_{>0})$ and $b=-\max(A\cap\mathbb Z_{<0})$ Let $u=\gcd(a,b)$ $\exists$ nonnegative integers $m,n,p,q$ such that $ma+n(-b)=u$ and $pa+q(-b)=-u$ Then , using c3, ge get that $u,-u\in A$ and so $u+(-u)=0\in A$ , impossible And so $\boxed{\text{No such function}}$

stem_md: Let  $k$  be a positive integer. Show that exists positive integer  $n$ , such that sets  $A = \{ 1^2, 2^2, 3^2, ...\}$  and  $B = \{1^2 + n, 2^2 + n, 3^2 + n, ... \}$  have exactly  $k$  common elements.
solution_md:
Here is an other solution I found:
For a positive integer  $n$ ,let  $d(n)$  be the number of positive divisors of  $n$  and  $f(n)$  be the number of pairs  $(a,b)$  such that  $n=a^2-b^2$ .Problem asks to prove that  $f(n)$  is surjective.We prove the following claim:**Claim:**
If  $n$  is an odd,non-square positive integer,then  $d(n)=2f(n)$ .**Proof:**
If for two positive integers  $a,b,n=a^2-b^2$  then  $n=(a-b)(a+b)$ ,so there is a divisor  $d$  of  $n$  such that  $a-b=d,a+b=\frac{n}{d}$ .Now,its enough to prove that every pair  $(d,\frac{n}{d})$  gives a unique and distinct pair of  $(a,b)$ .Of course,since  $n$  is odd, $d+\frac{n}{d}$  is even and such  $a,b$  exist and  $a=\frac{d^2+n}{2d}$ .Assume that there is a positive divisor  $t$  of  $n$  with  $t>d$  such that  $\frac{d^2+n}{2d}=\frac{t^2 +n}{2t}$  so:  $$ t d^2 +tn=d t^2 +dn \implies (t-d)n=(t-d)dt \implies n=dt \implies t=\frac{n}{d} $$  .
So each pair  $(d,\frac{n}{d})$  gives a distinct pair  $(a,b)$  with  $n=a^2-b^2$  and obviously,these are the only solutions,so  $d(n)=2f(n)$ .Since the function  $d(n)$  is surjective on even numbers(even with odd non-square entries,this follows immediately from the formula of  $d(n)$ ) so  $f(n)$  is also surjective and we are done.

We are effectively looking for  $n$  such that there are exactly  $k$  pairs  $(x,y) \in \mathbb{N}^2$  with:  $$ y^2=x^2+n \Leftrightarrow (y-x)(y+x)=n $$  Setting  $n=2^{2(k+1)}$  we must have:  $$ x+y=2^{l} \quad \quad y-x=2^{2k+2-l} $$  . 
Giving:  $$ x=\frac{2^l-2^{2k+2-l}}{2} \quad \quad y=\frac{2^l+2^{2k+2-l}}{2} $$  As  $x,y$  are positive integers we must have  $l>2k+2-l \Leftrightarrow l \geq k+2$ . We must also have  $2k+2-l>0 \Rightarrow l \leq 2k+1$  so there are:  $$ (2k+1)-(k+2)+1=k $$  Pairs  $(x,y)$  satisfying the condition so we're done.

stem_md: $n$  ( $n \ge 4$ ) green points are in a data space and no  $4$  green points lie on one plane. Some segments which connect green points have been colored red. Number of red segments is even. Each two green points are connected with polyline which is build from red segments. Show that red segments can be split on pairs, such that segments from one pair have common end.
solution_md:
Let  $\boldsymbol{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E})$  be a graph from the problem and let  $\boldsymbol{T}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}')$  be its spanning tree. I will denote by  $d(X)$  the degree of  $X$  in  $\boldsymbol{G}$  and by  $t(X)$  the degree of  $X$  in  $\boldsymbol{T}$ .  By taking the longest path of this tree we arrive at two cases
(1) There exists a path  $A-B-C$ , where  $t(A)=1, t(B)=2$ . Then we pair vertices  $\{A,B \}, \{B,C\}$ . We delete those edges from  $\boldsymbol{G}$ . If  $d(A)=1$ , then we delete  $A$  from  $\boldsymbol{G}$ , otherwise the removal of  $\{A,B\}$  doesn't disconnect  $\boldsymbol{G}$ . Same for  $B$ . In all cases we got a subgraph of  $\boldsymbol{G}$  with sctrictly less edges and possibly less vertices, but the number of edges is even and it remains connected.
(2) Otherwise there is a vertice  $C$  (the second last vertices on the found longest path) and  $t(C) \geq 3$ , it is a father of at least two leaves  $A,B$ . If  $\{ A,B\} \in \mathcal{E}$ , we can substitute edge  $\{ C,A\}$  with  $\{ A,B\}$  in the spanning tree, which leads to case one. Otherwise we pair up edges  $\{A,C\},\{B,C\}$  and delete the from  $\boldsymbol{G}$ . If  $d(A)=1$ , we delete  $A$ , otherwise it has a neighbour  $D \neq B$  in  $\boldsymbol{G}$ . Same for  $B$ . In the case we at least one of the vertices, say  $A$ , is not deleted we still get a conncted graph  $\boldsymbol{G}$  because we  $A$  is connected to  $D \neq B$  in  $\boldsymbol{G}$ .  In all cases  we got a subgraph of  $\boldsymbol{G}$  with sctrictly less edges and possibly less vertices, but the number of edges is even and it remains connected.

Inductively, using this method, we will pair up all vertices correctly.

stem_md: Let  $a$  and  $b$  be the positive integers. Show that at least one of the numbers  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $a+b$  can be expressed as the difference of the squares of two integers.
solution_md:
<details><summary>solution</summary>It is well-known that:
- All odd integers can be expressed as a difference of squares since  $2k+1=(k+1)^2-k^2$ - All multiples of  $4$  can be expressed as a difference of squares since  $4k=(k+1)^2-(k-1)^2$ If one of  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $a+b$  is odd, then we are done. Hence, assume that  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $a+b$  are all even. Clearly, we cannot have  $a \equiv b \equiv a+b \equiv 2 \pmod{4}$ . Thus, one of  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $a+b$  must be a multiple of  $4$ , so we are also done.   $\blacksquare$</details>

stem_md: Let  $a$ ,  $b$ , and  $d$  be positive integers. It is known that  $a+b$  is divisible by  $d$  and  $a\cdot b$  is divisible by  $d^2$ . Prove that both  $a$  and  $b$  are divisible by  $d$ .
solution_md: We assume that $\gcd(a, b, d) = k$ , and let $a = a'k$ , $b = b'k$ , and $d = d'k$ , where it is clear that $\gcd(a', b', d') = 1$ . Now we know that $d'^2 \mid a'b'$ and $d' \mid a' + b'$ . We claim that $d' = 1$ . Proof: Assume that $d' > 1$ . Then, there exists a prime number $p$ such that $p \mid d'$ . Thus, we have $$ p \mid a'b' \rightarrow p \mid a' \text{ or } p \mid b'. $$ Without loss of generality, assume $p \mid a'$ . Then we have: $$ p \mid a' + b' \rightarrow p \mid b'. $$ Thus, we get $p \mid a', b', d' \rightarrow p \mid \gcd(a', b', d') = 1$ , which leads to a contradiction. Therefore, we conclude that $d' = 1$ , which implies that $$ d = k \rightarrow d = \gcd(a, b, d) \rightarrow d \mid a, b. $$ The statement of the problem is thus proved. :)

Is it possible to do this in such a way that every two of these eight sums are different? Justify your answer.
solution_md: The answer is NO.  Assume that it is possible. Let the row sums are  $2^a, 2^b, 2^c, 2^d$  and column sums are  $2^p, 2^q, 2^r, 2^s$  where  $a,b,c,d,p,q,r,s$  are all different. Now, the total sum  $= 2^a+2^b+2^c+2^d=2^p+2^q+2^r+2^s$   WLOG, assume that  $a<b<c<d$  and  $p<q<r<s$    $\implies 2^a(1+2^{b-a}+2^{c-a}+2^{d-a})=2^p(1+2^{q-p}+2^{r-p}+2^{s-p})$  Clearly both the expressions inside the brackets are odd as the eight numbers are different, hence  by equating the order of 2  $\implies 2^a=2^b \implies a=b$ , which contradicts our initial assumption. So, there is no such configuration.

stem_md: Each integer should be colored by one of three colors, including red. Each number which can be represent as a sum of two numbers of different colors should be red. Each color should be used. Is this coloring possible?
solution_md:
Each integer should be colored by one of three colors, including red. Each number which can be represent as a sum of two numbers of different colors should be red. Each color should be used. Is this coloring possible?
Integers are $\ldots, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots $ . So it is not possible. Let the three colors be red, green, blue. Let $R$ , $G$ , $B$ the set of integers with color red, green, blue. Suppose that $0 \in R$ . Then for any $g \in G$ , $g=g+0 \in R$ , a contradiction. Hence we have $0 \not \in R$ . Without loss of generality, we may assume that $0 \in G$ . Pick $b \in B$ . Then $b=b+0 \in R$ , an absurdity. Hence we cannot color all integers in such a manner.

stem_md: Let  $ABC$  be an acute traingle with  $AC \neq BC$ . Point  $K$  is a foot of altitude through vertex  $C$ . Point  $O$  is a circumcenter of  $ABC$ . Prove that areas of quadrilaterals  $AKOC$  and  $BKOC$  are equal.
solution_md:
Let  $L$  be the foot from  $O$  to  $AB$ .  $[AKOC] = \frac{AK \cdot KC}{2} + \frac{KC \cdot KL}{2} = \frac{KC(AK + KL)}{2} = \frac{KC \cdot AL}{2}$ .
Now we just have to prove that its area is equal to  $[BKOC]$ .

Notice that  $[BKOC] = [KBC] - [KOC] = \frac{(BK \cdot KC) - (KC \cdot KL)}{2} = \frac{KC(BK - KL)}{2} = \frac{KC \cdot LB}{2} = \frac{KC \cdot AL}{2} = [AKOC]$ , so we're done.  $\square$

First equation gives $x=yz+1$ and second equation becomes $y=\frac{2-z}{z^2+1}$ This implies : Either $z>2$ and $z^2+1\le z-2$ , impossible Either $z=2$ and so $y=0$ and $x=1$ Either $z<2$ and so $z^2+1\le 2-z$ and so $z\in\{-1,0\}$ , from which only $z=0$ fits, giving $y=2$ and $x=1$ Hence the result $\boxed{(x,y,z)\in\{(1,0,2),(1,2,0)\}}$

stem_md: Each integer has been colored in one of three colors. Prove that exist two different numbers of the same color, whose difference is a perfect square.
solution_md: Suppose contrary and let  $n\in Z$ . Then  $n+16,n$  have different colors,  $n+25,n$  have different colors and  $n+25,n+16$  have different colors. So a triple  $n,n+16,n+25$  has three-colors.  $n+9$  can't have a color of  $n, n+25$  hence it's colored as  $n+16$ . So every two numbers that their difference is  $7$  are colored the same. Hence every two different numbers that their difference is divisible by  $7$  have the same color. In particular  $49-0=7^2$ . So numbers  $49,0$  have the same color. Contradiction.

stem_md: The integers  $a, b, c$  are not  $0$   such that  $\frac{a}{b + c^2}=\frac{a + c^2}{b}$ . Prove that  $a + b + c \le 0$ .
solution_md:
$$ \frac{a}{b+c^2}=\frac{a+c^2}{b} $$      $$ ab=(a+c^2)(b+c^2) $$      $$ ab=ab+ac^2+bc^2+c^4 $$      $$ c^2(a+b+c^2)=ab-ab=0 $$  Now,we will only look at the case when  $a+b+c^2=0$ ,because the other case implies  $c^2=0\Rightarrow c=0$  which we cannot have,so:  $$ a+b+c^2=0\Rightarrow c^2=-a-b $$   Let  $a_1$  and  $b_1$  be integers such that  $a=-a_1$  and  $b=-b_1$   $$ c^2=a_1+b_1\Rightarrow c=\sqrt{a_1+b_1}=({a_1+b_1})^\frac{1}{2}\leq{(a_1+b_1)}^1=a_1+b_1 $$     $$ \Rightarrow c\leq a_1+b_1 $$  Multiplying the last expression by  $-1$  we have: $-c\geq -a_1-b_1=a+b$   $<=>$   $a+b+c\leq 0$  
Q.E.D

stem_md:
Positive integers  $a, b, c$  have the property that: $\bullet$   $a$  gives remainder  $2$  when divided by  $b$ , $\bullet$   $b$  gives remainder  $2$  when divided by  $c$ , $\bullet$   $c$  gives remainder  $4$  when divided by  $a$ .
Prove that  $c = 4$ .
solution_md:
Let  $a = bx + 2,b = cy + 2, c = az + 4$ . $c = az + 4 = (bx + 2)z + 4 = ((cy + 2)x + 2)z + 4 = cxyz + 2xz + 2z + 4$ Obviously we must have  $x, y \geq 1$  since  $a > 4$  and  $b > 2$ . $c(xyz - 1) + 2xz + 2z + 4 = 0$ So we must have  $c(xyz-1)<0$ , but since  $c>0$ , we have  $xyz < 1$ .
Since  $x,y \geq 1$ , we can only have  $z = 0$  and so  $c = 4$ .

stem_md:
The  $14 \times 14$  chessboard squares are colored in pattern, as shown in the picture. Can you choose seven fields blacks and seven white squares of this chessboard in such a way, that there is exactly one selected field in each row and column? Justify your answer.
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/e/4/e8ba46030cd0f0e0511f1f9e723e5bd29e9975.png)
solution_md:
solved with navi_09220114
Suppose yes.
Notice that the square  $(i, j)$  is white if  $i + j$  is even and black if  $i + j$  is odd.
Define sequence  $a$  such that  $(i, a_{i})$  is a colored square where  $1 \leq i \leq 14$ .
So we want there to be 7 numbers such that  $n+a_{n}$  is odd and 7 numbers such that  $n + a_{n}$  is even.
So  $\sum^{14}_{i=1}(i+a_{i})$  must be odd since it is a sum of 7 odd numbers and 7 even numbers.
But, since  $1 \leq a_{i}\leq 14$  and  $a_{i} \neq a_{j}$  for  $i \neq j$ , the sequence  $a$  is just a permutation of  $\{1, 2, 3, \dots, 14\}$ .
So  $\sum^{14}_{i=1}i + \sum^{14}_{i=1}a_{i} = 2 \times \sum^{14}_{i=1}i$  is odd, but this is a contradiction as it means that a number is both even and odd.
So the answer is no.

stem_md: The integer  $n \geq 1$  does not contain digits:  $1,\; 2,\; 9\;$  in its decimal notation. Prove that one of the digits:  $1,\; 2,\; 9$  appears at least once in the decimal notation of the number  $3n$ .
solution_md:
[tip=Hint]
In fact, you only have to look at the first digit.
[/tip]
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We prove the contrapositive: if none of the digits 1, 2, or 9 appear in  $3n$ , then  $n$  must contain at least one of  $1, 2, 9$ .

Consider the first digit of  $3n$  (which clearly is nonzero): if it is either 3, 4, or 5, then  $n$  must have a first digit of  $1$ . If it is either 6, 7, or 8, then  $n$  must have a first digit of  $2$ . Thus, if none of the digits  $1, 2, 9$  appear at least once in the decimal representation of  $3n$ , then  $n$  must have a first digit of either  $1$  or  $2$ . Thus, if  $n$  does not contain  $1, 2, $  or  $9$ , then since we can't have none of the digits appearing at least once, at least one of them must appear in  $3n$ . Yay! :DD</details>

stem_md: Find all triples  $(a,b,c)$  of nonzero integers for which \[(1-a)(1-b)(1-c)=(1+a)(1+b)(1+c).\]
solution_md:
Take  $a \le b \le c$ . If  $a > 1$ , we get LHS negative and RHS positive. If  $c < -1$ , we get LHS positive and RHS negative. 

If  $b=1$ , then  $a=-1$  and  $c$  can be anything. If  $c=1$ , then  $a$  or  $b$  equal to  $-1$  and the other can be anything. These are all our solutions and we prove them to be the only ones.

We now consider  $a<-1$  and  $c>1$  as  $a$  and  $c$  are nonzero and  $c=1$  or  $a=-1$  cases have been dealt with.
We now have that  $(1-a) > 0$ ,  $(1+a) < 0$ ,  $(1-c) < 0$  and  $(1+c) > 0$ . Therefore,  $(1-b)$  and  $(1+b)$  must have the same sign, meaning  $b=0$ , but that isn't allowed.

Therefore, all the solutions are with  $a \le b \le c$ :  $(a,b,c) = (-1,-1,1), (-1,1,1), (-r,-1,1), (-1,1,r)$  with  $r > 1$  an integer.

stem_md: In each square of a  $10\times 10$  board, there is an arrow pointing upwards, downwards, left, or right. Prove that it is possible to remove  $50$  arrows from the board, such that no two remaining arrows point at each other.
solution_md:
Let's call it a *pair* when two arrows are pointing at each other. There are  $100$  arrows in the board, so at most there can be  $50$  *pairs* in the entire board. Removing one arrow from each *pair* should break up all the *pairs* and leave no two arrows pointing at each other, unless the subset of arrows pointing in one direction in any given row or column is larger than the subset of arrows pointing at them within that row or column. This would make it so that removing an arrow from the larger set would not decrease the total number of *pairs* in the board. To prevent this, always remove an arrow from the smaller of the two subsets when breaking up a *pair*.

Essentially, remove the smallest subset of arrows from every row and column that has at least one other arrow within that row or column pointing at it. If both subsets are equal, get rid of either.

stem_md: Let  $n\geq 3$  be an odd integer. On a line,  $n$  points are marked in such a way that the distance between any two of them is an integer. It turns out that each marked point has an even sum of distances to the remaining  $n-1$  marked points. Prove that the distance between any two marked points is even.
solution_md: <details><summary>solution</summary>Let the integer points be at distances  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{n}$ . Observe that the even sum condition modulo  $2$  is the same as  $\sum_{i} a_i \equiv na_i \pmod 2$  for all  $a_i$ . Since  $n$  is odd, this implies that  $a_i \equiv a_j \pmod 2$  for all  $i, j$ ; implying that the distance between any two marked point is even.</details>

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer. Each of the numbers  $1,2,3,\ldots,100$  is painted with one of  $n$  colors in such a way that two distinct numbers with a sum divisible by  $4$  are painted with different colors. Determine the smallest value of  $n$  for which such a situation is possible.
solution_md:
If we have  $2$  numbers  $x$  and  $y$  such that  $x\equiv y \equiv 0 \text{ or } 2\mod 4$ , then  $x$  and  $y$  must be different colors. Thus, since there are  $25$  numbers in each residue class,  $n$  must be at least  $25$ .

It is easy to see that  $25$  is possible if we use a unique color for each pair of numbers  $4k-2$  and  $4k$  where  $k$  is a positive integer less than or equal to  $25$ , and then select  $2$  distinct colors that have already been used, one to color all the numbers  $ x \equiv 1 \mod 4$  and one to color all the numbers  $x \equiv 3 \mod 4$ .

solution_md:
Solution:
Real numbers $a,b,c$ satisfy $a+b \ne 0$ , $b+c \ne 0$ and $c+a \ne 0$ . Show that \[\left(\frac{a^2c}{a+b}+\frac{b^2a}{b+c}+\frac{c^2b}{c+a}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{b^2c}{a+b}+\frac{c^2a}{b+c}+\frac{a^2b}{c+a}\right) \ge 0.\]
From T2 Lemma: $\frac{a^2c}{a+b}+\frac{b^2a}{b+c}+\frac{c^2b}{c+a} = \frac{a^2}{\frac{1}{c}(a + b)} + \frac{b^2}{\frac{1}{a}(b + c)} + \frac{c^2}{\frac{1}{b}(a + c)} \geq \frac {(a + b + c)^2}{\frac{1}{c}(a + b) + \frac{1}{a}(b + c) + \frac{1}{b}(a + c)}$ $\frac{b^2c}{a+b}+\frac{c^2a}{b+c}+\frac{a^2b}{c+a} = \frac{b^2}{\frac{1}{c}(a + b)} + \frac{c^2}{\frac{1}{a}(b + c)} + \frac{a^2}{\frac{1}{b}(a + c)} \geq \frac {(b + c + a)^2}{\frac{1}{c}(a + b) + \frac{1}{a}(b + c) + \frac{1}{b}(a + c)}$ So $$ (\frac{a^2c}{a+b}+\frac{b^2a}{b+c}+\frac{c^2b}{c+a}) * (\frac{b^2c}{a+b}+\frac{c^2a}{b+c}+\frac{a^2b}{c+a}) \geq (\frac {(a + b + c)^2}{\frac{1}{c}(a + b) + \frac{1}{a}(b + c) + \frac{1}{b}(a + c)})^2 \geq 0 $$
You cannot apply Titu's lemma, since the denominators $\frac{a+b}{c}$ etc. need to be positive. In general, I doubt there is a solution using this lemma.

Let  $S=\underbrace{111\dots 1}_{19}\underbrace{999\dots 9}_{19}$ . Show that the  $2S$ -digit number
\[\underbrace{111\dots 1}_{S}\underbrace{999\dots 9}_{S}\]
is a multiple of  $19$ .
solution_md: <details><summary>solution</summary>$N=\underbrace{111\dots 1}_{S}\underbrace{999\dots 9}_S$  $N=\dfrac{10^{2S}-1}{9}+8 \cdot \dfrac{10^S-1}{9}=\dfrac{(10^S-1)(10^S+9)}{9}$  $19 \mid N$  if and only if  $S \in \{0,1\} \pmod {18}$  $S \equiv 1 \pmod 2, S \equiv 1 \pmod 9 \Longrightarrow S \equiv 1 \pmod {18}$</details>

stem_md: A party is attended by boys and girls. Each person attending the party knows exactly 3 boys and exactly 7 girls among the other people. Prove that the number of all the people attending the party is divisible by 20.
solution_md: <details><summary>sol</summary>We represent the problem as a graph (vertices are people, edges represent two people knowing each other), and first consider the boys and the girls separately. Among the boys, every boy knows 3 other boys, which means the number of boys is even. Likewise, the number of girls is also even. Now, we consider the amount of edges between a boy and a girl. Let's say there are  $x$  boys and  $y$  girls. Each boy knows  $7$  girls, so there are  $7x$  such edges. Each girl knows  $3$  boys, so there are  $3y$  edges. Therefore, we have  $7x=3y.$  This means that  $x=3a$  and  $y=7a$  for a positive integer  $a.$  However, remember that we know that the number of boys and girls are even, so we have  $a=2b$  for some positive integer  $b$ , since both  $3$  and  $7$  are odd. Therefore,  $x=6b$  and  $y=14b$ , so  $x+y=20b$ , so we are done.</details>

stem_md: Find all primes  $(p, q, r)$  such that   $$ pq+4=r^4. $$
solution_md:
$pq = r^4 - 4 = (r^2 - 2)(r^2 + 2)$ . We have that either  $r^2 - 2$  is  $1$  or  $pq$ , or that it is  $p$  or  $q$ . It cannot be  $1$  and it cannot be  $pq$  either because that would imply that  $r^2 + 2 = 1$ , impossible. Therefore,  $WLOG$    $p \leq q$ . We obtain: $r^2 - 2 = p$ . *(1)* $r^2 + 2 = q$ . *(2)*

We now have primes with a difference of  $4$ . If  $p = 2 \implies q = 6$ , but  $q$  would not be prime. If it was  $p = 3 \implies r^2 = 5$ , which is impossible. Therefore,  $p > 3$ , and it's well known that for every prime  $p > 3$ ,  $p \equiv \pm 1 \mod 6$ . Using this fact, if  $p \equiv -1 \mod 6 \implies q \equiv -1 + 4 \equiv 3 \mod 6$ . However, this is not possible because  $q > 3$ , therefore  $p \equiv 1 \mod 6$  and  $q \equiv -1 \mod 6$ . Now, adding *(1)* and *(2)* we notice that: $2r^2 = p + q$ . Taking this expression  $\mod 6$  we notice that  $2r^2 \equiv p + q \equiv 1 - 1 \equiv 0 \mod 6$ . This implies that  $r^2$  has a factor of  $3$ , so the only possibility is that  $r = 3$ , which immediately implies that  $p = 7$  and  $q = 11$ . Therefore, our only solutions are  $\boxed{(7, 11, 3); (11, 7, 3)}$  which indeed satisfy the problem.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Poland Contests/Polish Junior Math Olympiad/2025 Polish Junior Math Olympiad/2025 Polish Junior Math Olympiad Finals/3528314.json

stem_md: Inside the circle of radius  $1$  there are points  $A_1, A_2, A_3, ..., A_{100}$ . Prove that there is one point  $P$  at the edge of the circle  for which  $P A_1 + P A_2 + ... + P A_{100} \ge 100$ .
solution_md: Consider two antipodes of the circle,  $P$  and  $Q.$  By the triangle inequality,  $\sum_{i=1}^{100} PA_i + A_iQ \ge 100 PQ = 200.$  Therefore,  $\left(\sum_{i=1}^{100} P A_i \right)+ \left(\sum_{i=1}^{100} Q A_i\right) \ge 200,$  so one of these two sums is at least  $100$  as desired.

stem_md: Is there a tetrahedron in which at least one face is an obtuse triangle and the center of the sphere circumscribed around this tetrahedron lies in its inside? Justify your answer.
solution_md:
Ah, daily dose of geo, thanks as always!  :)
<details><summary>Related:</summary>[https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OkmNXy7er84](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OkmNXy7er84)
And no, this is not a rickroll, this is a 3b1b video which I think has cool relations to this problem (and is my motivation for the solution below)</details>

<details><summary>sol</summary>Yes.
Explanation:
On a fixed sphere  $\omega$ , create an obtuse triangle  $ABC$  whose vertices lie on sphere  $\omega$  and whose plane does not pass through the center of the sphere, which we will call  $O$ . Now, draw lines  $AO$ ,  $BO$ , and  $CO$ . Suppose they intersect  $\omega$  again at  $X$ ,  $Y$ , and  $Z$ . Now, on the section of  $\omega$  encased by arcs  $XY$ ,  $XZ$  and  $YZ$ , pick  $D$ , which we are always able to do. Now, it is clear that tetrahedron  $ABCD$  contains  $O$  because  $DO$  must intersect  $\triangle{ABC}$ . Then, since  $\triangle{ABC}$  is obtuse, the conditions are met.</details>

stem_md: Given is the square  $ABCD$  of side  $1$  and a straight line  $\ell$ passing through his center. Let  $a, b, c, d$  denote the distances of points  $A, B, C, D$ , respectively from line  $\ell$ . Prove that  $a^2+ b^2+ c^2+ d^2=1$ .
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>This problem can be easily solved with the point-to-line distance formula. Say that the square has its center at the origin. Now, scale up the whole shape by  $2$ , which makes the numbers nicer, but we must remember to scale things down at the end. That means that the square has vertices of  $(1,1), (1,-1), (-1,-1),$  and  $(-1,1)$ . Say that the line has equation  $-mx+y=0$ . We now simply have to use the point to line formula on each one, square them, and add them together:  $$ (\frac{-m+1}{\sqrt{m^2+1}})^2+(\frac{-m-1}{\sqrt{m^2+1}})^2+(\frac{m+1}{\sqrt{m^2+1}})^2+(\frac{m-1}{\sqrt{m^2+1}})^2 \implies $$    $$ \frac{m^2-2m+1}{m^2+1}+\frac{m^2+2m+1}{m^2+1}+\frac{m^2+2m+1}{m^2+1}+\sqrt{m^2-2m+1}{m^2+1} \implies $$    $$ \frac{4m^2+4}{m^2+1}=4 $$  But, since we scaled everything up by  $2$  at the start we must divide by  $2^2=4$  at the end, getting us that  $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$  is indeed  $\boxed{1}$ .</details>

stem_md:
Segments  $AD$  and  $BE$  are the altitudes of the acute triangle  $ABC$ . On the outside of the triangle  $ABC$ , were built the square  $ABKL$  and thre rectangles  $BDMN$  ,  $AEPQ$ , with  $BN = BC$  and  $AQ = AC$ . Prove that the sum of the areas of the rectangles  $BDMN$  and  $AEPQ$  is equal to the area of the  square  $ABKL$ .
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/5/c/3588749d0637f0a1ccbdf1fee45469ca7c87ed.png)
solution_md: <details><summary>sol</summary>Let  $AB$ ,  $AC$ , and  $BC$  be  $c$ ,  $b$ , and  $a$ . Furthermore, let  $\angle ACB=\theta$ . By Law of Cosines:   $$ c^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos(\theta) $$     $$ \iff c^2=a(a-b\cos(\theta))+b(b-a\cos(\theta)) $$   Notice that  $a\cos(\theta)=CE$  and  $b\cos(\theta)=CD$ . Therefore,  $b-a\cos(\theta)=AE$  and  $a-b\cos(\theta)=BD$ . Therefore,   $$ c^2=a(BD)+b(AE) $$   as desired.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Poland Contests/Polish Junior Math Olympiad/Poland Juniors - Geo/Poland Juniors  Round 1 - geometry/2514324.json

stem_md: Point  $P$  lies on the sphere circumscribed around a cube. Prove that sum of squares of distances of point  $P$  from the vertices of the cube does not depend on the choice of point  $P$ .
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>For any two diametrically opposite points on a sphere, any third point will form a right angle with them. Hence, by the Pythagorean Theorem, the sum of the squares of the distances from  $P$  to each pair of opposite vertices of the cube equals the square of the space diagonal. This means the sum of the squares of all  $8$  vertices equals  $4$  times the square of the space diagonal, or  $12s^2$ , where  $s$  is the side length of the cube.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Poland Contests/Polish Junior Math Olympiad/Poland Juniors - Geo/Poland Juniors  Round 1 - geometry/2516007.json

stem_md:
A convex quadrilateral  $ABCD$  is given. The points  $K$  and  $L$  are by the midpoints of the sides  $AB$  and  $CD$ , respectively. Show that if the areas of the quadrilaterals  $BCLK$  and  $DAKL$  are equal, then the quadrilateral  $ABCD$  is a trapezoid.
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/6/0/c5652fc161a582a6e66189b7a42a2535ae1a86.png)
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Let the line through  $D$  parallel to  $AB$  intersect line  $KL$  and  $P$  and line  $BC$  at  $Q$ . By similar triangles,  $P$  is the midpoint of  $DQ$ .  Hence by trapezoid areas,  $\text{[}ADPK\text{]} = \text{[}BKPQ\text{]}$ , so the area condition is equivalent to  $\text{[}PDL\text{]}=\text{[}QCLP\text{]}$ . But by similar triangles again,  $\text{[}PDL\text{]}=\frac{1}{3}\text{[}QCLP\text{]}$ , so they can only be equal if they are both equal to  $0$ , or when  $CD\parallel AB$ , as desired.</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Poland Contests/Polish Junior Math Olympiad/Poland Juniors - Geo/Poland Juniors  Round 1 - geometry/2516011.json

An equilateral triangle  $ABC$  is inscribed in the circle  $o$ . Point  $D$  lies on the shorter arc  $BC$  of circle  $o$ . Point  $E$  is symmetrical to point  $B$  wrt line  $CD$ . Prove that points  $A, D, E$   lie on one straight line.
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/a/2/a49eb22a31ab180baa4f2cb7e2f2dcd2e341e0.png)
solution_md:
<details><summary>Sol.</summary>Because $ D\in o$ ,  $ABCD$  is an cyclic quadilateral, hence  $\angle CDA= \angle B =60^{\circ}$ , and  $\angle CDB = 180^{\circ} - \angle A=120^{\circ}$ . Also, CBE is an isosceles thus CB=CE and CD is the angle bisector of  $\angle BCE$  so  $\triangle CDB = \triangle CDE$  hence  $\angle CDE =\angle CDB= 120^{\circ}$  . 
In the end we have  $\angle ADE = \angle ADC+ \angle CDE= 60^{\circ} +120^{\circ}= 180^{\circ}.$  q.e.d.</details>

stem_md:
On both sides of the river with parallel banks, there are two houses  $A$  and  $B$ , with the line  $AB$  not perpendicular to the banks of the river (see figure). Where should the bridge be built, perpendicular to the river banks, that the roads from both houses to the bridge, running in a straight line, were of equal length? Give the appropriate construction with a compass and a ruler and justify its correctness.
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/5/6/7819211d490fac72713daad6a56edc1a129f51.png)
solution_md:
<details><summary>Rough Construction</summary>Ker idea:  Remove the river from the picture.

Step 1.  Let the river width be  $w$ .  Translate  $A$  upwards  $w$  units to  $A'$ .  Now let the upper shoreline of the river be the line  $L$ .

It suffices to find a point  $x$  on  $L$  that is equidistant from  $A$  and  $B$ .

Step 2.  Draw the perpendicular bisector of  $\overline{A'B}$  and mark its intersection  $x$  with  $L$ .  We are done.</details>

stem_md:
Inside the square  $ABCD$ , point  $P$  is selected such that  $AP = AB$  and  $\angle CPD = 90^o$ . Prove that  $DP = 2CP$ .
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/e/c/c646131d3a8c19f77327ebbb494eff777542fd.png)
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Join  $B,P$ . As, $AP=AB=AD$  $\implies A$  is the circumcenter of  $\triangle BPD$ Let, $\angle PDB=\theta$ , so, $\angle PAB=2\theta$ So, $\angle APB=\angle ABP=\frac{180^\circ-2\theta}{2}=90^\circ-\theta$ So, $\angle DBP=45^\circ-\theta$ Again, $\angle PDC=45^\circ-\theta$  $\implies \angle PCD=45^\circ+\theta$ So, $\angle PCB=45^\circ-\theta$ And  $\angle PBC=45^\circ-\angle DBP=\theta$ So,in  $\triangle DBP$  and in  $\triangle BCP$  $\angle PBC=\angle PDB=\theta$  $\angle PBD=\angle PCB=45^\circ-\theta$  $\implies \triangle DBP\sim CBP$ So, $\frac{BP}{DP}=\frac{CP}{BP}=\frac{BC}{BD}=\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}$  $\implies DP=\sqrt 2 BP$ And,  $BP=\sqrt 2CP$ So, $DP=\sqrt 2\cdot \sqrt 2\cdot CP=2CP \blacksquare$</details>

A triangle  $ABC$  is given where  $\angle ACB = 60^o$  . The circle  $o$  is cirxumscribed around this triangle. Point  $X$  is the midpoint of this arc  $BC$   of circle  $o$  that does not include point  $A$ , and point  $Y$  is the midpoint of this arc  $CA$  of circle  $o$ , that does not contain point  $B$ . Prove that the line   $XY$  is tangent to the inscribed circle into triangle  $ABC$ .
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/a/f/20e5e10c107e976cb5808843d61bdfd6228437.png)
solution_md:
<details><summary>Please Say Somebody,Am I right?</summary>Let  $AX$  and  $BY$  intersect at  $I$ . So,  $I$  is the incenter of  $\triangle ABC$ .Let   $E\in AB$  and  $F\in XY$  such that  $IE\perp AB$  and  $IF\perp XY$ . Here  $IE$  is the in-radius of  $\triangle ABC$ .
Now, $\angle AIB=90^\circ+\frac{60^\circ}{2}=120^\circ$ So, $\angle XIB=\angle YIA=60^\circ$ Again, $\angle AXB=\angle AYB=60^\circ$ So, $\triangle AIY$  and  $\triangle BIX$  both are equilateral. 
So,in  $\triangle AIB$  and in  $\triangle XIY$  $AI=YI,BI=XI,\angle AIB=\angle XIY$ So, $\triangle AIB\cong \triangle XIY$  $\implies AB=XY$ So,area of   $\triangle AIB$ =area of  $\triangle XIY$ So  $\frac {1}{2} \cdot AB\cdot IE=\frac{1}{2}\cdot XY\cdot IF$  $\implies IE=IF$ So, $IF$  is also inradius.
So,  $F$  lies in the incircle.  $XY$  passes through  $F$  and the inradius  $IF\perp XY$  by construction.  $\implies XY$  is tangent to the incircle  $\square$</details>

stem_md:
The quadrilateral  $ABCD$  is inscribed in a circle where  $\angle ABC = 60^o$  and  $BC = CD$ . Prove  $AB = AD + DC$ .
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/4/a/467ebcd606cf26ab7c2ac3fe1c3e1aa55604e8.png)
solution_md:
Note that arc  $AC$  has measure  $120$ .
If arc  $DC$  has measure  $x$ , then arc  $AB$  has measure  $240-x$  and arc  $AD$  has measure  $120-x$ The length of  $AB$  is  $$ 2r\sin (120-\frac{x}{2}) $$    $$ \boxed{2r\sin(60+\frac{x}{2})} $$  The length of  $AD+DC$  is  $$ 2r(\sin(60-\frac{x}{2})+\sin\frac{x}{2}) $$    $$ 2r(\sin(120+\frac{x}{2})+\sin\frac{x}{2}) $$  Using sum to product identities, this expression is equivalent to   $$ 2r\sin(60+\frac{x}{2}) $$

We equate these to get
\begin{align*}
AB^2+BC^2-2AB\cdot BC\cos(60) &= AD^2+CD^2-2AD\cdot CD\cos(120) 
AB^2+BC^2-AB\cdot BC &= AD^2+CD^2+AD\cdot CD 
AB^2+CD^2-AB\cdot CD &= AD^2+CD^2+AD\cdot CD 
AB^2-AB\cdot CD &= AD^2+AD\cdot CD 
AB^2-AD^2 &= (AB+AD)CD 
(AB-AD)(AB+AD) &= (AB+AD)CD 
AB-AD &= CD
\end{align*}

The rectangle  $ABCD$  is given. The points  $E$  and  $F$  lie on the sides of  $BC$  and  $CD$ , respectively, with  $\angle EAF = 45^o$  and  $BE = DF$ . Show that the area of triangle  $AEF$  is equal to the sum the areas of triangles  $ABE$  and  $ADF$ .
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/c/1/93a597c94d384961bcc8d5939bc63f879a36b7.png)
solution_md: $A = (0, 0)$  $B = (1, 0)$  $C = (1, a)$  $D = (0, a)$  $E = (1, b)$  $F = (c, a)$  $BE = DF \iff b = c$  $\angle EAF = 45^{\circ}, BE = DF \iff ab + b^{2} - a + b = 0$  or  $ab - b^{2} + a + b = 0$  (notice that  $ab - b^{2} + a + b = 0$  is impossible else  $ab < ab + a + b < b^{2} < ab$  which implies that  $ab < ab$ ) $[AEF] = [ABE] + [ADF] \iff ab + b^{2} + b - a = 0 \iff \angle EAF = 45^{\circ}, BE = DF$

stem_md:
The points  $K, L, M$  lie on the sides  $BC, CA, AB$ , respectively of equilateral triangle  $ABC$  and satisfy the conditions  $KM = LM$ ,  $\angle KML = 90^o$  and  $AM = BK$ . Prove that  $\angle CKL = 90^o$ .
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/9/7/cfa0f1180f0751947baa58c635dcbde1fd1aaf.png)
solution_md: <details><summary>Click to expand</summary>By law of sines we have  $\frac{sin(60)}{LM} = \frac{sin(ALM)}{AM}$  then using triangle  $KMB$  we now  $\frac{sin(60)}{KM} = \frac{sin(KMB)}{KB}$  now given the side lengths we know are equal we can see that  $sin(ALM) = sin(KMB)$  and by exterior angle theorem  $ALM + 60 = 90 + KMB$  this tells us that  $ALM \neq KMB$  but we know that the sin is equal so then we know  $ALM = 180 - KMB$  plugging this into the equation giving us  $KMB = 75$  using exterior angle theorem again we know  $KMB + KBM = LKM + CKL$  we know all of these angles except  $CKL$  giving us  $75 + 60 = 45 + CKL$  giving us  $CKL = 90$ .</details>

Points  $X$  and  $Y$  lie on sides  $AC$  and  $BC$ , respectively, of triangle  $ABC$ . Point  $M$  is the midpoint of segment  $XY$ . Suppose  $AX = MX = MC = MY = BY$ . Find the measure of angle  $\angle AMB$ .

solution_md: $MX = MC = MY$  gives a right angle at  $C$  (Thales). From the Exterior angle theorem in the isosceles triangles  $AMX$  and  $BMY$  follows $|\angle AMX| + |\angle BMY| = \frac{1}{2}\left( |\angle MXC| + |\angle MYC| \right) = \frac{1}{2}\left( 180^{\circ} - |\angle XCY| \right) = 45^{\circ}$ and therefore  $|\angle AMB| = 180^{\circ} - |\angle AMX| - |\angle BMY| = \boxed{135^{\circ}}$ .

Given a cuboid  $ABCDA'B'C'D'$  with vertices labeled as in the figure, where  $AC'=AB+AD$ . Let  $P$  be a point on the segment  $AC'$  such that  $AP =AB$  and  $C'P =AD$ . Prove that  $\angle BPB'=90^o$ .
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/d/b/a62c0632c9e4ab2d7bc91d2dae3059a284d3e4.png)
solution_md:
Given the cuboid  $\stackrel{A'B'C'D'}{A\,B\,C\,D}\ :\ A(d,b,0),B(0,b,0),C(0,0,0),D(d,0,0),B'(0,b,\sqrt{2bd}),C'(0,0,\sqrt{2bd})$ ,
satisfying the distance  $AC'=b+d$ .

We find the point  $P(\frac{bd}{b+d},\frac{b^{2}}{b+d},\frac{d\sqrt{2bd}}{b+d})$ .
The direction numbers of  $PB\ :\ (\frac{bd}{b+d},-\frac{bd}{b+d},\frac{d\sqrt{2bd}}{b+d})$ ,
the direction numbers of  $PB'\ :\ (\frac{bd}{b+d},-\frac{bd}{b+d},-\frac{b\sqrt{2bd}}{b+d})$ . $PB\ \bot\ PB'$ , because  $\frac{bd}{b+d} \cdot \frac{bd}{b+d} +(-\frac{bd}{b+d}) \cdot (-\frac{bd}{b+d}) +\frac{d\sqrt{2bd}}{b+d} \cdot (-\frac{b\sqrt{2bd}}{b+d})=0$ .

Arek has a piece of paper in the shape of a rhombus  $ABCD$ , in which  $\angle BCD = 90^o$ . First, he folds it so that the segments  $CB$  and  $CD$  coincide on the line  $CA$ , and then so as to obtain a triangle as shown in the figure.  Prove that the distances from point  $A$  to all three vertices of the resulting triangle are equal.
![Image](https://cdn.artofproblemsolving.com/attachments/6/4/a211606cdab206f5ce20aef2acf226294337f6.png)
solution_md:
Given the square  $ABCD\ :\ A(-1,0),B(1,0),C(0,1),D(0,-1)$ .

@above that is not true, it looks like you made a silly. If we have  $a=c$ , then  $$ \frac{1}{4}(ab+bc)=\frac{1}{2}ba $$  This would imply that the angle between  $b$  and  $a$  is  $90$ . However, since  $a=c$ , we require that 2 of the angles are  $90$ , which is not possible.

<details><summary>solution</summary>The area of the triangle is  $\frac{1}{2}ba\sin C=\frac{1}{2}bc\sin A$ .
Taking the average of those 2 terms, we have that the area is  $$ \frac{1}{4}(ab\sin C+bc\sin A) $$  Since  $0\leq\sin A,\sin C\leq 1$ , we have that   $$ \frac{1}{4}(ab\sin C+bc\sin A)\leq \frac{1}{4}(ab+bc) $$  with equality when  $\sin A=\sin C=1$ .
However, this only occurs when  $A=C=90$ , which is not possible</details>

stem_md: Point  $M$  is the midpoint of side  $AB$  of  $ABC$  with  $\angle BAC + \angle MCB = 90^o$  Show that the triangle  $ABC$  is isosceles or right.
solution_md: <details><summary>sol</summary>Let  $\angle{ABC}=\beta$  and let  $\angle BAC =\alpha$ . Therefore,  $\angle BCM=90-\alpha$  so  $\angle BMC = 90+\alpha-\beta$ . From here,  $\angle AMC = 90+\beta-\alpha$  which makes  $\angle ACM = 90-\beta$ . Now let  $CM=d$  and let  $AM=MB=a$ . By Law of Sines on  $\triangle AMC$    $$ \frac{a}{\sin(\alpha)}=\frac{b}{\cos(\beta)} $$     $$ \frac{a}{b}=\frac{\sin(\alpha)}{\cos(\beta)} $$   Now, by Law of Sines on  $\triangle BMC$    $$ \frac{a}{\sin(\beta)}=\frac{b}{\cos(\alpha)} $$     $$ \frac{a}{b}=\frac{\sin(\beta)}{\cos(\alpha)} $$   Therefore,   $$ \frac{\sin(\beta)}{\cos(\alpha)}=\frac{\sin(\alpha)}{\cos(\beta)} $$     $$ \sin(\beta)\cos(\beta)=\sin(\alpha)\cos(\alpha) $$     $$ \sin(2\beta)=\sin(2\alpha) $$   Since  $90-\alpha$  is an angle in this figure,  $\alpha<90$ . Similarly,  $\beta<90$ . This implies that  $2\beta=2\alpha$  or  $2\beta=180-\alpha$ . In other words,  $\beta=\alpha$  corresponding to an isosceles triangle, or  $\beta=90-\alpha$ , corresponding to a right triangle.</details>

stem_md: Point  $E$  lies on side  $CD$  of rectangle  $ABCD$ , with   $$ \angle DAE+\angle EBC=\angle ABE.  $$  Prove that  $AB\ge AD$ .
solution_md: We have  $$ \angle EAD+\angle CBE=\angle EBA, $$  which gives  $$ 90^\circ -\angle BAE +90^\circ -\angle EBA =\angle EBA, $$  which gives  $$ 180^\circ -\angle BAE-\angle EBA=\angle EBA, $$  which gives  $$ \angle AEB=\angle EBA, $$  which gives  $$ AE=AB. $$  We have  $AE\geq AD$  because it's the hypothenuse of the (possibly degenerated) right triangle  $ADE$ . Anyway, here is the solution:

Extend AB, CD to meet at X, and AF, DE to meet at Y. Then triangles XBC and YEF are isosceles. Thus AX + DY = AB + BX + DE + EY = AF + CD + CX + FY = AY + DX. So AXDY has an inscribed circle, say with centre O. The perpendicular bisectors of BC and EF are just the angle bisectors of angle BXC, angle EYF respectively; these pass through O. On the other hand note that angle BXC = angle EYF, so XO = YO (angle between tangents depends monotonically on distance to origin). The reflection across the angle bisector of angle XOY thus swaps X and Y, but fixes the inscribed circle (since the axis of reflection passes through the centre O). So it swaps the tangents from X to the circle with the tangents from Y to the circle, which means it fixes A and D, their intersections. Thus AD is this axis of reflection, and so passes through O.

The line  $BC\ :\ y=\sqrt{3}(x-b)$ , then  $G(g,\sqrt{3}(g-b)\ )$ .
The line  $FA\ :\ y=-\sqrt{3}x$ , then  $J(b-g,\sqrt{3}(b-g)\ )$ . $GJ=a \Rightarrow g=\frac{a+b}{2}$ .

Point  $C(\frac{3b}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}b}{2})$ .
The line  $CD\ :\ y-\frac{\sqrt{3}b}{2}=-\sqrt{3}(x-\frac{3b}{2})$ , then  $H(g,\frac{\sqrt{3}b}{2}-\sqrt{3}(g-\frac{3b}{2})\ )$ . $GH=a \Rightarrow a=(3-\sqrt{3})b$ .

stem_md: What algebraic relationship holds between  $ \alpha $ ,  $ \beta $  and  $ \gamma $  when the equality is satisfied  $$  \tan \alpha + \tan \beta + \tan \gamma = \tan \alpha \tan \beta \tan \gamma? $$
solution_md:
$\tan(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=\frac{\tan \alpha+\tan \beta+\tan \gamma-\tan \alpha\tan \beta\tan \gamma}{1-\tan \alpha\tan \beta-\tan \beta\tan \gamma-\tan \gamma\tan \alpha}$ . $\tan(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)=0$ , $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=k \cdot \pi$
You need to address this case: $$ \tan\alpha\tan\beta+\tan\beta\tan\gamma+\tan\gamma\tan\alpha = 1 $$ because $\tan(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)$ turns into $\frac{0}{0}$ .
Click to expandThere are no solutions to the following system: $$ \tan \alpha + \tan \beta + \tan \gamma = \tan \alpha \tan \beta \tan \gamma $$ $$ \tan\alpha\tan\beta+\tan\beta\tan\gamma+\tan\gamma\tan\alpha = 1 $$ Let $r_1=\tan\alpha$ , $r_2=\tan\beta$ , $r_3=\tan\gamma$ be the roots of a monic cubic polynomial. By Vieta's formulas, the cubic is $$ t^3-(r_1+r_2+r_3)t^2+(r_1r_2+r_2r_3+r_3r_1)t-r_1r_2r_3. $$ Since $r_1+r_2+r_3=r_1r_2r_3$ and $r_1r_2+r_2r_3+r_3r_1=1$ , we can rewrite this cubic as $$ t^3-r_1r_2r_3t^2+t-r_1r_2r_3=(t^2+1)(t-r_1r_2r_3). $$ This cubic has only $1$ real solution, but $\tan\alpha$ , $\tan\beta$ , $\tan\gamma$ (3 real numbers) are its roots. Contradiction.
Btw I found this thread because [2025 HMMT Alg/NT #7](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c129h3501445p34018813) builds on this problem.

stem_md: Prove that if a quadratic equation  $$  ax^2 + bx + c = 0 $$  with integer coefficients has a rational root, then at least one of the numbers  $ a $ ,  $ b $ ,  $ c $  is even.
solution_md:
Let  $x=\frac{p}{q} (p, q \in \mathbb{Z}, gcd(p,q)=1)$  be a rational root to  $ax^2+bx+c=0$ .  This results in: $a\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)^2 + b\left(\frac{p}{q}\right) + c = 0  \Rightarrow ap^2 + bpq +cq^2=0$  (i).

There are two cases to consider for coprime  $p, q$ : (1)  $p, q$  both odd and (2)  $p$  even (odd),  $q$  odd (even).  If  $p$  &  $q$  are both odd, then (i) can never equal  $0$  if  $a, b, c$  are also odd.  Therefore, at least one of them must be even.  If  $p$  is even &  $q$  is odd, then  $c$  must be even in order for (i) to equal  $0$ .   If  $p$  is odd &  $q$  is even, then  $a$  must be even in order for (i) to equal  $0$ .  

QED

stem_md: Prove that if  $ n $  is an integer greater than  $ 4 $ , then  $ 2^n $  is greater than  $ n^2 $ .
solution_md:
Prove by induction. Take base case of  $n = 5$ . Clearly, this is true. 
Now we induct. Assume  $2^n > n^2$ , with  $n > 4$ . Then,  $2^{n+1} = 2^n * 2 > 2n^2 = n^2 + n^2 > n^2 + 2n + 1 = (n+1)^2$ . So, we are done. 

(To show that  $n^2 > 2n+1$  is just the same as  $(n-1)^2 > 2$ , which is clearly true)

stem_md: Prove that the inequality   $$  \frac{1}{3} \leq \frac{\tan 3\alpha}{\tan \alpha} \leq 3  $$   is not true for any value of  $ \alpha $ .
solution_md:
Equivalent to  $\frac 13 \leq \frac{2\cos(2\alpha)+1}{2 \cos (2\alpha) -1} \leq 3$ . 
Take  $x = \cos(2\alpha)$ , which is bounded in  $(-1, 1)$ , giving  $\frac 13 \leq \frac{2x+1}{2x-1} \leq 3$ .
This is a function with vertical asymptote at  $x = \frac 12$ . We can see this function is constantly decreasing. Hence, just plug in  $x = -1, 1$ , and we are done.

stem_md: Prove that if the integers  $ a $  and  $ b $  satisfy the equation  $$  2a^2 + a = 3b^2 + b, $$  then the numbers  $ a - b $  and  $ 2a + 2b + 1 $  are squares of integers.
solution_md:
Here's a number-theoretic solution. 

If  $a=b$ , we are done as  $a=b=0$ . So, suppose  $a
e b$ . Let  $d={m gcd}(a,b)$  with  $a=da_1$  and  $b=db_1$ . We obtain  $d(3b_1^2 - 2a_1^2) = a_1-b_1$ . Now I claim  $3b_1^2-2a_1^2=1$ . Suppose this is not the case and let  $p\mid 3b_1^2-2a_1^2$  be a prime (check that  $a_1
e b_1$  as  $a
e b$ ). We have  $p\mid a_1-b_1$ . Then  $3b_1^2-2a_1^2\equiv a_1^2\equiv 0\pmod{p}$ . So,  $p\mid a_1$ . Likewise,  $p\mid b_1$ . Combining, we get  $p\mid (a_1,b_1)=1$ , a contradiction. Hence,  $3b_1^2-2a_1^2=\pm 1$ . The case  $3b_1^2-2a_1^2=-1$  would yield  $a_1^2\equiv -1\pmod{3}$ , a contradiction. So,  $3b_1^2-2a_1^2=1$ . Thus,  $a_1-b_1=d$  so  $a-b=d^2$  and  $2a+2b+1=2d(a_1+b_1)+1 = 2a_1^2-2b_1^2+1 = b_1^2$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Poland Contests/Polish MO Finals/1965 Polish MO Finals/3390106.json

candidates:
Solving our Diophatine equation for  $a$  yields: $a = \frac{-1 \pm\sqrt{1-4(2)(-3b^2-b)}}{4} = \frac{-1 \pm \sqrt{24b^2+8b+1}}{4}$  (i).

If  $a \in \mathbb{Z}$ , then the discriminant in (i) must be a square integer, or: $24b^2+8b+1 = A^2 \Rightarrow b = \frac{-8 \pm \sqrt{64-4(24)(1-A^2)}}{48} = \frac{-2 \pm \sqrt{6A^2-2}}{12}$  (ii).

If  $b \in \mathbb{Z}$ , then the discriminant in (ii) must also be a square integer, or: $6A^2-2 = B^2  \Rightarrow 6A^2 - B^2 = 2 \Rightarrow A^2 = 1, B^2 = 4$  (iii).

Substitution of (iii) into (ii) yields  $b = \frac{-2 \pm 2}{12} = 0, -\frac{1}{3}$ , of which  $b = 0$  is admissible.  A final substitution of this value for  $b$  into (i) gives us  $a = \frac{-1 \pm 1}{4} = 0, -\frac{1}{2}$ , of which  $a = 0$  is admissible.  Hence,  $a-b=0$  and  $2a+2b+1=1$ ....both are squares of integers.

QED

We consider only the nontrivial case:  $a \neq b \neq 0$ .
From the given equation we get  $(3(a+b)+1)(a-b)=a^2$  and  $(2(a+b)+1)(a-b)=b^2$ .
Multiplying both sides of these equations we obtain $(3(a+b)+1)(2(a+b)+1)(a-b)^2=(ab)^2$ .
Hence  $(3(a+b)+1)(2(a+b)+1)$  must be a square integer.
Noting that  $(3(a+b)+1, 2(a+b)+1)=1$ , it follows that both   $3(a+b)+1$  and  $2(a+b)+1$  are square integers, hence  $a-b$  must be a square integer as well.

stem_md: Prove that for every natural  $n$   $$ \frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{3\cdot 5} + \frac{3}{3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7} + ...+ \frac{n}{3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot  ...\cdot (2n+1)} < \frac{1}{2}. $$
solution_md:
Prove that for every natural $n$ $$ \frac{1}{3} + \frac{2}{3\cdot 5} + \frac{3}{3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7} + ...+ \frac{n}{3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 \cdot ...\cdot (2n+1)} < \frac{1}{2}. $$
We have $\frac{2k}{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2k + 1)} = \frac{1}{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2k - 1)} - \frac{1}{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2k + 1)}$ so $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{2k}{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2k + 1)} = 1 - \frac{1}{1 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdots (2n + 1)}<1$ .

stem_md:
Let  $s \geq 3$  be a given integer. A sequence  $K_n$  of circles and a sequence  $W_n$ 
of convex  $s$ -gons satisfy:
\[ K_n \supset W_n \supset K_{n+1}  \] for all  $n = 1, 2, ...$ 
Prove that the sequence of the radii of the circles  $K_n$  converges to zero.
solution_md:
This is an inmediate consecuence of the following fact: if inside a circle you have a convex s-gon, and inside this s-gon you have another circle, then the radius of the inner circle is at most  $\frac{1+\cos\frac{\pi}{s}}{2}$  times the radius of the outer circle. So the radius of  $K_1, K_2, \dots$  form a sequence bounded by above for a geometric sequence of ratio less than zero.
The mentioned fact is easy to prove. Consider inside a circle of radius 1 another circle of radius  $r$ ,  $r>\frac 1 2$ , then the circle concentric with the first one and radius  $2r-1$  is also inside both circles. But if this radius  $2r-1>\cos\frac\pi s$  is easy to prove that any chord of the outermost circle subtending an angle of at least  $\frac{2\pi}n$  intersects the innermost circle, so that  $2n$  segments between the outermost and the innermost circles cannot close to form an s-gon.

stem_md: Show that for every convex polygon there is a circle passing through three consecutive vertices of the polygon and containing the entire polygon
solution_md:
I think this won't be entirely clear, but I'm sure you can see what's going on. 

Take a circle of minimal radius containing the polygon. There are two situations: either two of the vertices of the polygon are antipodes in this circle, and the rest are inside, or at least three vertices of the polygon lie on thye circle. These two cases are essentially the same in what follows, so assume WLOG that  $A_i,A_j,A_k$  are vertices of the polygon  $A_1A_2\ldots A_n$  on the circle.

At least one of  $|i-j|,|j-k|,|k-i|$  is  $\ge 2$  (assume the polygon has at least four vertices), so assume it's  $|i-j|$ . Now keep the circle passing through  $A_i,A_j$ , and move it "towards" the portion of the polygon between  $A_i,A_j$  which does not contain  $A_k$  until it meets some other vertex  $A_{i_1}$  of the polygon, between  $A_i,A_j$ . If  $A_i,A_{i_1},A_j$  are not consecutive, at least one of  $|i-i_1|,|i_1-j|$  is  $\ge 2$ , and, if we assume WLOG it's  $|i-i_1|$ , we can keep the circle passing through  $i,i_1$  and move it "towards" the portion of the polygon between  $A_i,A_{i_1}$  until it meets some other vertex  $A_{i_2}$ , between  $A_i,A_{i_1}$ , and so on.

stem_md: Consider the polynomial  $W(x) = (x - a)^kQ(x)$ , where  $a \neq 0$ ,  $Q$  is a nonzero polynomial, and  $k$  a natural number. Prove that  $W$  has at least  $k + 1$  nonzero coefficients.
solution_md:
WLOG, we may assume that $W(0)\ne 0$ (we simply divide $W$ by $x^n$ for the largest possible exponent $n$ ; the number of non-zero coefficients does not change). Now we can prove the assertion by induction on the degree of the polynomial. If $n$ is the degree of $W$ , the degree of $W'$ is $n-1$ , and $(x-a)^{k-1}|W'(x)$ . This means, according to the induction hypothesis, that $W'$ has at least $k$ non-zero coefficients, and these correspond to $k$ non-zero coefficients of $W$ . Furthermore, the free term of $W$ is a non-zero coefficient which does not appear in $W'$ , so we're done.
Nice, but to make it formal you need to prove it if $k=1$

stem_md: The function  $f : R \to R$  satisfies  $f(3x) = 3f(x) - 4f(x)^3$  for all real  $x$  and is continuous at  $x = 0$ . Show that  $|f(x)| \le 1$  for all  $x$ .
solution_md:
The function $f : R \to R$ satisfies $f(3x) = 3f(x) - 4f(x)^3$ for all real $x$ and is continuous at $x = 0$ . Show that $|f(x)| \le 1$ for all $x$ .
Setting $x=0$ in equation implies $f(0)\in\left\{-\frac{\sqrt 2}2,0,\frac{\sqrt 2}2\right\}$ all values in $(-1,1)$ . Note that $|x|\le 1$ $\iff$ $|3x-4x^3|\le 1$ So $|f(x)|>1$ $\implies$ $|f(\frac x3)|>1$ And so sequence $\left\{f(\frac x{3^n})\right\}$ has all its elements out of $[-1,+1]$ and so can never have a limit in $(-1,1)$ And since we previously claimed that $f(0)\in(-1,1)$ , this shows that $f(x)$ is not continuous at zero. Hence the conclusion $\boxed{|f(x)|\le 1\quad\forall x}$

$p(x,y)$  is a polynomial such that  $p(cos t, sin t) = 0$  for all real  $t$ . 
Show that there is a polynomial  $q(x,y)$  such that  $p(x,y) = (x^2 + y^2 - 1) q(x,y)$ .
solution_md:
Let  $P(x, y) = (x^2 + y^2 - 1)Q(x, y) + xR(y) + S(y)$  
 
We have   $$ P(\cos t, \sin t) = \cos t R(\sin t) + S(\sin t) $$      $$ P(\cos (\pi - t), \sin (\pi - t)) = \cos (\pi - t) R(\sin (\pi - t)) + S(\sin (\pi - t)) = - \cos t R(\sin t) + S(\cos t) $$

stem_md: Find the maximum possible volume of a tetrahedron which has three faces with area  $1$ .
solution_md: Let  $a$  be the length of the longest edge bordering the two faces of unit area. It's easy to check that  $a\ge \sqrt{2}$ . Let  $\varphi$  be the dihedral angle of edge  $a$ . Using the formula  $V=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{S_1S_2}{a}\sin \varphi$  for the volume of the tetrahedron where  $S_1$  and  $S_2$  are the areas of the triangles sharing the edge  $a$  we conclude that  $$ V=\frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{\sin\varphi}{a}\le \frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3} $$  This value is reached when the tetrahedron has three pairwise orthogonal edges of length  $\sqrt{2}$  emanating from the same vertex.

stem_md:
$p$  is a prime and  $m$  is a non-negative integer  $< p-1$ . 
Show that  $ \sum_{j=1}^p j^m$  is divisible by  $p$ .
solution_md: Denote  $A(p,k)=\sum_{j=1}^p j^k$  for all non-negative integers  $k$ . Induction: for  $k=0$  we have  $A(p,0)=p$ . Assume  $\exists_{l\in \lbrace 0,1,...,p-2\rbrace}\forall_{k\in\lbrace 0,1,...,l\rbrace}p|A(p,k)$ . $(j+1)^{l+1}-j^{l+1}=\sum_{n=0}^l{l+1\choose n}j^n$  $(p+1)^{l+1}-1^{l+1}=\sum_{j=1}^p\left((j+1)^{l+1}-j^{l+1}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^p\sum_{n=0}^{l+1}{l+1\choose n}j^n=\sum_{n=0}^{l+1}{l+1\choose n}\sum_{j=1}^pj^n=(l+1)A(p,l+1)+\sum_{n=0}^{l}{l+1\choose n}A(p,n)$ From here  $p|A(p,l+1)$  is clear.

stem_md: The real numbers  $x_1, x_2, ... , x_n$  belong to the interval  $(0,1)$  and satisfy  $x_1 + x_2 + ... + x_n = m + r$ , where  $m$  is an integer and  $r \in [0,1)$ . Show that  $x_1 ^2 + x_2 ^2 + ... + x_n ^2 \leq m + r^2$ .
solution_md:
Allow the variables  $x_k$  to also take values  $0$  and  $1$ , at the ends of the interval  $(0,1)$ . Then the function  $E(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n) = \sum_{k=1}^n x_k^2$  is continuous, defined on the compact domain  $\left \{(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)  \in [0,1]^n \mid \sum_{k=1}^n x_k = m+r \right \}$ , thus by Weierstrass' theorem it reaches its maximum.

Say  $x,y$ , two of the coordinates of a point in the domain, are such that  $0< x \leq y < 1$ ; then for  $\varepsilon = \min\{x,1-y\} > 0$  we have  $(x-\varepsilon) + (y+\varepsilon) = x+y$  and  $(x-\varepsilon)^2 + (y+\varepsilon)^2 = x^2+y^2 + 2\varepsilon(y-x) + 2\varepsilon^2 > x^2+y^2$ , hence that point cannot be a point of maximum.

It follows the maximum can only be reached at a point where some  $a$  coordinates are equal to  $x = 0$ , some  $b$  coordinates are equal to  $y = 1$ , and at most one other coordinate  $z$  is in  $[0,1)$ . From the restriction we immediately get that  $z=r$ ,  $b=m$  and  $a=n-m-1$ . The value at such a point is then  $E = a\cdot 0 + b\cdot 1 + r^2 = m+ r^2$ , precisely the one claimed. We thus have proven the claim, and also found the equality cases.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Poland Contests/Polish MO Finals/1988 Polish MO Finals/56456.json

stem_md: For a permutation  $P = (p_1, p_2, ... , p_n)$  of  $(1, 2, ... , n)$  define  $X(P)$  as the number of  $j$  such that  $p_i < p_j$  for every  $i < j$ . What is the expected value of  $X(P)$  if each permutation is equally likely?
solution_md:
Let  $A_j$  be the event that  $p_1$ ,  $p_2$ ,  $\ldots$ ,  $p_{j-1}$  are all less than  $p_j$ .  That event is equivalent to  $p_j$  being the maximum of  $p_1$ ,  $p_2$ ,  $\ldots$ ,  $p_j$ .  By symmetry, the probability of that event is  $\frac{1}{j}$ .

By linearity of expecation, the expected value of  $X$  is
\[ E(X) = \sum_{j=1}^n \Pr(A_j) = \sum_{j=1}^n \frac{1}{j} \, .  \]
In other words, the answer is the  $n$ th harmonic number.

stem_md: $W$  is a polygon which has a center of symmetry  $S$  such that if  $P$  belongs to  $W$ , then so does  $P'$ , where  $S$  is the midpoint of  $PP'$ . Show that there is a parallelogram  $V$  containing  $W$  such that the midpoint of each side of  $V$  lies on the border of  $W$ .
solution_md:
It's useful to have seen [this problem](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?t=35947) before :).

For compactness reasons, there is a parallelogram  $ABCD$  of minimal area containing the polygon  $\cal W$  (and which has the center of symmetry  $O$  of  $\cal W$  as its own center of symmetry). Let's prove that such a polygon satisfies the requirements. 

Suppose, for instance, that the midpoints  $M,N$  of  $AD,BC$  (respectively) do not belong to the border  $\partial\cal W$  of  $\cal W$ . The intersection between  $\partial\cal W$  and  $AD$  is a closed (maybe degenerate) segment  $s$  which lies either in  $[AM)$  or  $(MD]$ . Suppose it's the former. Then, the intersection  $\partial\cal W\cap BC$  will be a closed sgement  $s'$  which lies in  $(NC]$ . Now keep  $M,N$  and the lines  $AB,CD$  fixed, and move  $A$  slightly, putting  $D=AM\cap CD$ , until  $AD$  no longer meets  $\partial\cal W$ , but such that  $ABCD$  still contains  $\cal W$  (a drawing should make all of this clear). Then  $BC$  will not meet  $\partial\cal W$  either, and the new parallelogram  $ABCD$  will have the same area as the old one. We can slightly shrink it along the direction of  $AB$  so that it still contains  $\cal W$ , and this contradicts the minimality of the area of the initial parallelogram.

stem_md: The sequence  $a_1, a_2, a_3, ...$  is defined by  $a_1 = a_2 = a_3 = 1$ ,  $a_{n+3} = a_{n+2}a_{n+1} + a_n$ . Show that for any positive integer  $r$  we can find  $s$  such that  $a_s$  is a multiple of  $r$ .
solution_md:
Does anyone actually understand Singular's solution?  :what?: 


Anyways, the idea for this problem is the same idea used to show that for any  $r$ , we can find a Fibonacci number divisible by  $r$ .


Note that each term is dependent only on the previous three terms. In  $\mathbb{Z}/r\mathbb{Z}$ , there are only finitely many possibilities for a ordered triple. Thus by Pigeonhole principle, there exist some positive integers  $p < q$  such that  $(a_p, a_{p+1}, a_{p+2}) \equiv (a_q, a_{q+1}, a_{q+2}) \pmod r$ . Since three consecutive terms uniquely determine this doubly-infinite sequence (since the recursion  $a_{n+3} = a_{n+2}a_{n+1} + a_n$  can be applied both forward and backward), the sequence must be periodic  $\pmod r$  with period  $T = q - p$ . Since  $a_0 = 0$ , we have  $a_T \equiv 0 \pmod r$ , as desired.

stem_md:
On a  $2004 \times 2004$  chess table there are 2004 queens such that no two are attacking each other\footnote[1]{two queens attack each other if they lie on the same row, column or direction parallel with on of the main diagonals of the table}.

Prove that there exist two queens such that in the rectangle in which the center of the squares on which the queens lie are two opposite corners, has a semiperimeter of 2004.
solution_md:
Let's look at that problem I mentioned earlier:

For  $i\in\overline{0,n-1}$ , let  $\sigma(i)-i$  denote the distance modulo  $n$ , in a counter-clockwise direction, between  $i$  and  $\sigma(i)$ . If we assume that all  $\sigma(i)-i$  are distinct, it means that they are  $0,1,\ldots,n-1\pmod n$ . If we add all these quantities, we get something which is not divisible by  $n$  (it's  $\frac n2\cdot(n-1)\pmod n$ ), but, on the other hand,  $\sum(\sigma(i)-i)=0\pmod n$  because the residues  $\{\sigma(i)\}$  are the same as the residues  $\{i\}$ , so we have a contradiction. This means that there are  $i,j$  s.t.  $\sigma(i)-i=\sigma(j)-j\pmod n$ . This proves the assertion, I believe.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/National and Regional Contests/Poland Contests/Polish MO Finals/1989 Polish MO Finals/34679.json
